'''Sunnyside''' is a neighborhood in the western portion of the [[New York City]] [[Borough (New York City)|borough]] of [[Queens]]. It is bounded by [[Hunters Point, Queens|Hunters Point]] and [[Long Island City]] to the west, [[Astoria, Queens|Astoria]] to the north, [[Woodside, Queens|Woodside]] to the east, and [[Maspeth, Queens|Maspeth]] and [[Newtown Creek]] to the south. The [[Sunnyside Yard]] rail complex separates the neighborhood from Astoria along its northern boundary, and the [[Brooklyn–Queens Expressway]] forms part of its southern edge.

The area developed as a residential bedroom community in the years after the [[Queensboro Bridge]] opened in 1909 and the [[IRT Flushing Line|Flushing Line]] subway reached Queens in 1917. Most of the neighborhood was built up between the early 1920s and the late 1930s. North of [[Queens Boulevard]], the planned community of [[Sunnyside Gardens, Queens|Sunnyside Gardens]] was constructed between 1924 and 1928 as one of the first applications of the [[Garden city movement|garden-city]] model in the United States; it was listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]] in 1984 and designated a New York City historic district in 2007. Sunnyside is served by the {{NYCS trains|Flushing local}} subway and is along the route of the annual [[St. Pat's for All]] parade.

Sunnyside is located in [[Queens Community Board 2|Queens Community District 2]], and its [[ZIP code]]s are 11101, 11104, and 11377.<ref name="NYCPlanning"/> It is patrolled by the [[New York City Police Department]]'s 108th Precinct.<ref name="NYPD 108th Precinct"/> Politically, Sunnyside is represented by the [[New York City Council]]'s 26th District.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nyc.gov/html/dc/downloads/pdf/queens.pdf|title=Current City Council Districts for Queens County|publisher=New York City|access-date=May 5, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161222003335/http://www.nyc.gov/html/dc/downloads/pdf/queens.pdf|archive-date=December 22, 2016}}</ref>

==Geography==
The neighborhood is located in western [[Queens]]. It is bounded by the [[Long Island Rail Road]] [[Main Line (Long Island Rail Road)|Main Line]] and [[Sunnyside Yard]] to the north and by the [[Brooklyn–Queens Expressway]] and [[Newtown Creek]] to the south.<ref name="Franklin2020">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/11/18/realestate/sunnyside-queens.html|title=Sunnyside, Queens: The Lure of Greenery in a Pandemic|last=Franklin|first=Sydney|date=November 18, 2020|work=The New York Times|access-date=May 29, 2026}}</ref> Sources differ on the neighborhood's eastern and western extent; for example, ''The Encyclopedia of New York City'' gives Van Dam Street as the western boundary and [[Calvary Cemetery (Queens)|Calvary Cemetery]] and 51st Street as the eastern boundary,<ref name="Jackson1266"/> whereas a ''New York Times'' article gives boundaries at 39th Street to the west, and to the east by 48th Street south of Queens Boulevard and 52nd Street north of Queens Boulevard.<ref name="Franklin2020"/> The [[New_York_City_Department_of_City_Planning|Department of City Planning's]] 2020 Neighborhood Tabulation Area (NTA) for Sunnyside occupies approximately {{convert|1095|acre|ha}}.<ref name="DCP2020NTAArea">{{cite web |title=2020 Neighborhood Tabulation Areas (NTAs) |website=NYC Open Data |publisher=New York City Department of City Planning |url=https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/2020-Neighborhood-Tabulation-Areas-NTAs-/9nt8-h7nd |access-date=June 2, 2026 |id=Socrata dataset 9nt8-h7nd |quote=Row where ''nta2020''=QN0202 (Sunnyside, Queens): ''shape_area'' = 47,701,718.40 (square feet, in the NAD83 / New York Long Island US Survey Feet projection), equivalent to approximately 1,095 acres. |archive-date=April 4, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260404200651/https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/2020-Neighborhood-Tabulation-Areas-NTAs-/9nt8-h7nd |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Queens Boulevard]] runs through the middle of Sunnyside on a southwest-to-northeast diagonal and divides the neighborhood into two distinct residential areas. North of Queens Boulevard lies the [[Sunnyside Gardens, Queens|Sunnyside Gardens]] historic district, a planned community of brick rowhouses and small apartment buildings constructed between 1924 and 1928. South of Queens Boulevard includes prewar apartment buildings as well some houses, and residences south of Queens Boulevard tend to be larger and less expensive than residences north of it.<ref name="Franklin2020" /><ref name="Vandam2007">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/02/04/realestate/04livi.html|title=An Enclave at Once Snug and Inclusive|last=Vandam|first=Jeff|date=February 4, 2007|work=The New York Times|access-date=April 30, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200917000942/https://www.nytimes.com/2007/02/04/realestate/04livi.html|archive-date=September 17, 2020}}</ref> Queens Boulevard also marks the boundary between New York City Community School Districts 30 and 24.<ref name="CSD-boundaries">{{cite web |title=School District 24|publisher=Beta NYC |url=https://boundaries.beta.nyc/?map=sd&dist=24|access-date=2026-05-29}}</ref>

Sunnyside Yard, a {{convert|192|acre|ha|adj=on}} rail yard built by the [[Pennsylvania Railroad]] and opened in 1910, occupies the northern edge of the neighborhood and is now owned by [[Amtrak]] and shared with [[NJ Transit Rail Operations]].<ref name="Couper1912">{{Cite book|editor1-first=William|editor1-last=Couper|title=History of the Engineering, Construction and Equipment of the Pennsylvania Railroad Company's New York Terminal and Approaches|year=1912|publisher=Isaac H. Blanchard Co.|location=New York|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1Vs5AAAAMAAJ&pg=PP1|pages=76, 93}}</ref> The yard's deck has been the subject of repeated proposals for housing development above the active rails.<ref name="NYTRubinstein2026">{{cite news |last1=Rubinstein |first1=Dana |last2=Zaveri |first2=Mihir |last3=Chen |first3=Stefanos |date=February 27, 2026 |title=Can Mamdani (and Trump) Build a Neighborhood Over a Queens Rail Yard? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/27/nyregion/sunnyside-yard-mamdani-trump.html |work=The New York Times |access-date=May 29, 2026}}</ref> Calvary Cemetery is located south of the [[Brooklyn–Queens Expressway]] and abuts the southern and eastern edge of the neighborhood.

The principal commercial corridors are Queens Boulevard, [[Greenpoint Avenue]] between 39th and 49th Streets, and Skillman Avenue and 43rd Avenue.<ref name="SBS-CDNA">{{cite report |title=Commercial District Needs Assessment: Sunnyside |series=Avenue NYC |publisher=New York City Department of Small Business Services|date=2020|url=https://www.nyc.gov/assets/sbs/downloads/pdf/neighborhoods/avenyc-cdna-sunnyside.pdf |format=PDF |access-date=2026-05-29}}</ref>

==History==

===Pre-1909===
The area was farmed in colonial times by the Bragaw family, French Huguenot settlers who acquired land at Dutch Kills in 1690. During the [[American Revolutionary War|Revolution]], British forces occupied the Sunnyside area from 1776 to 1783, billeting troops in the colonial farmhouses along old Middleburgh Avenue (now 39th Avenue) to control the strategic "Narrow Passage" at the junction of present-day Northern Boulevard, Woodside Avenue, and Newtown Avenue.<ref name="Seyfried1984">{{Cite book|last=Seyfried|first=Vincent F.|title=300 Years of Long Island City, 1630–1930|year=1984|publisher=V.F. Seyfried|pages=79–81|url=http://vital.queenslibrary.org/vital/access/manager/Repository/aql:49|via=Queens Public Library Vital Resource Repository|access-date=April 30, 2026}}</ref> According to the local historian Vincent F. Seyfried, Richard Bragaw built a gambrel-roofed house "in the English style atop Sunnyside Hill" in 1790, on the line of present-day 32nd Place between Northern Boulevard and Skillman Avenue; the house was demolished in July 1903 after the [[Pennsylvania Railroad]] acquired the property as part of the land assembly for the [[Sunnyside Yard]].<ref name="Seyfried1984"/> A 1925 county history and a 2016 railroad history of Sunnyside Yard trace the area's name to "Sunnyside Hill," the Bragaw family estate established with that 1690 purchase and consolidated under Brocard's son Isaac in 1713.<ref name="HazeltonBoroughs1925">{{Cite book|editor-last=Hazelton|editor-first=Henry Isham|title=The Boroughs of Brooklyn and Queens, Counties of Nassau and Suffolk, Long Island, New York, 1609-1924|publisher=Lewis Historical Publishing Co.|location=New York|year=1925|page=946}}</ref><ref name="Morrison2016">{{Cite book|last1=Morrison|first1=David D.|last2=Quigley|first2=Stephen F.|title=Sunnyside Yard and Hell Gate Bridge|publisher=Arcadia Publishing|series=Images of Rail|year=2016|isbn=978-1-4671-2419-5|page=59}}</ref> ''The Encyclopedia of New York City'' alternatively traces the modern neighborhood's name to a roadhouse built on Jackson Avenue in the 1850s and 1860s for visitors to the Fashion Race Course in [[Corona, Queens|Corona]].<ref name="Jackson1266">{{Cite book|last=Jackson|first=Kenneth T.|title=The Encyclopedia of New York City|publisher=Yale University Press|year=2010|edition=2nd|isbn=978-0-300-11465-2|page=1266|title-link=The Encyclopedia of New York City}}</ref> South of Jackson Avenue, the Fitting, Gosman, Heiser, Lowery, and Van Buren families owned farms that were subdivided in the 1880s and 1890s, and a small hamlet built between Northern and Queens Boulevards came to be known as Sunnyside.<ref name="Jackson1266"/> The area was incorporated into [[Long Island City]] when that city was chartered on May 4, 1870, and into the [[City of Greater New York]] when Long Island City was consolidated into Greater New York on January 1, 1898.<ref name="Seyfried1984p102">{{Cite book|last=Seyfried|first=Vincent F.|title=300 Years of Long Island City, 1630–1930|year=1984|publisher=V.F. Seyfried|pages=102, 135|url=http://vital.queenslibrary.org/vital/access/manager/Repository/aql:49|via=Queens Public Library Vital Resource Repository|access-date=May 15, 2026|archive-date=October 21, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191021083840/http://vital.queenslibrary.org/vital/access/manager/Repository/aql:49|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 1901, the [[Irish American Athletic Club|Irish-American Athletic Club]] established [[Celtic Park (Queens)|Celtic Park]] near 48th Avenue and 43rd Street as a venue for [[Gaelic games]] and other Irish-American sporting events.<ref name="IrishTimesCelticPark">{{Cite news|url=https://www.irishtimes.com/sport/gaelic-games/celtic-park-where-the-new-york-irish-once-sported-and-played-drank-and-fought-1.4399106|title=Celtic Park – where the New York Irish once sported and played ... drank and fought|first=Dave|last=Hannigan|work=The Irish Times|date=November 5, 2020|access-date=April 30, 2026}}</ref> 

The [[Pennsylvania Railroad]] adopted a plan in 1901 for a large rail yard in the area, and between 1902 and 1905 it acquired the land south of Northern Boulevard between 21st and 43rd Streets, much of which was low-lying marshland.<ref name="Jackson1266"/> The Pennsylvania Railroad acquisitions and demolitions continued through 1905. Between 1907 and 1908, it leveled an approximately 200-acre hill at 34th and 35th Streets and used the earth to fill some 250 acres of tidal marsh at the headwaters of [[Dutch Kills]]. At its opening the largest [[coach yard]] in the world, Sunnyside Yard opened to rail traffic in November 1910, occupying {{convert|192|acre|ha}} and containing 25.7 miles of track.<ref name="Couper1912"/><ref name="Jackson1266"/>

===1909–1929===
The opening of the [[Queensboro Bridge]] in 1909 and the extension of the [[IRT Flushing Line|Flushing Line]] subway across [[Queens Boulevard]] in 1917 made Sunnyside accessible to Manhattan and triggered apartment construction.<ref name="Jackson1266"/> Through the 1920s, much of the area was built up, and the neighborhood became a [[bedroom community]] for middle-class workers commuting to Manhattan.<ref name="Vandam2007"/>

Industrial development accompanied the residential boom on land adjoining the new Sunnyside Yards: by 1912 the Degnon Terminal, a rail-served industrial complex developed by Michael J. Degnon's Degnon Terminal & Realty Company, was largely built out, with early tenants including the [[Loose-Wiles Biscuit Company]] (later [[Sunshine Biscuits]]), the [[Packard Motor Car Company]], the American Ever Ready Co., and the [[American Chicle Company]].<ref name="SeyfriedBoom">{{Cite book|last=Seyfried|first=Vincent F.|title=300 Years of Long Island City, 1630–1930|year=1984|publisher=V.F. Seyfried|chapter=The Boom Years 1898 through World War I|url=http://vital.queenslibrary.org/vital/access/manager/Repository/aql:49|via=Queens Public Library Vital Resource Repository|access-date=May 1, 2026|archive-date=October 21, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191021083840/http://vital.queenslibrary.org/vital/access/manager/Repository/aql:49|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1922 the [[Metropolitan Life Insurance Company]] broke ground on the Metropolitan Houses, an early Sunnyside multi-family apartment complex on the blocks bounded by Queens Boulevard, 48th Avenue, 48th Street, and 49th Street; the complex was later renamed Cosmopolitan Houses after Met Life sold the property, and portions remain federally subsidized.<ref name="WalshCosmopolitan2018">{{Cite web|url=https://forgotten-ny.com/2018/02/cosmopolitan-houses-woodside/|title=Cosmopolitan Houses, Woodside|last=Walsh|first=Kevin|website=Forgotten New York|date=February 20, 2018|access-date=May 1, 2026}}</ref>

Between 1924 and 1928, the City Housing Corporation, a limited-dividend organization led by developer [[Alexander Bing]], built [[Sunnyside Gardens, Queens|Sunnyside Gardens]] on a 77-acre site of about 16 blocks north of Queens Boulevard, between 43rd and 51st Streets. Architects [[Clarence Stein]], [[Henry Wright (planner)|Henry Wright]], and [[Frederick L. Ackerman]], working with landscape architect [[Marjorie Sewell Cautley]], designed the development as a [[Garden city movement|garden city]]–inspired community of low-rise attached brick houses arranged around shared interior courts. The development comprised 1,202 housing units and was the first major American application of the principles of [[Ebenezer Howard]] and [[Raymond Unwin]]. It was promoted by the [[Regional Planning Association of America]], whose members included [[Lewis Mumford]].<ref name="HDCSunnyside">{{Cite web|url=https://hdc.org/buildings/sunnyside-gardens-historic-district/|title=Sunnyside Gardens Historic District|publisher=Historic Districts Council|access-date=April 30, 2026|archive-date=January 16, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260116211413/https://hdc.org/buildings/sunnyside-gardens-historic-district/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Jackson1266"/><ref name="CityLore">{{Cite web|url=https://citylore.org/places/sunnyside-gardens/|title=Sunnyside Gardens|website=City Lore|access-date=April 30, 2026|archive-date=December 7, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251207024659/https://citylore.org/places/sunnyside-gardens/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Reflecting the neighborhood's growth over this decade, ridership at the [[40th Street%E2%80%93Lowery Street station|Lowery St. subway station]] increased from 256,080 in 1923 to 2,117,809 in 1930.<ref name="ThomsonHill1931">{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/57570517/|title=Thomson Hill Just Big Farm 7 Years Ago: Populous Queens Section Grew Like Bonanza Town After World War|last=Marzlock|first=Ron|work=Brooklyn Eagle|date=July 19, 1931|access-date=June 13, 2026|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

===1930–1960===
In 1931, the philanthropic Phipps Houses organization, founded by the family of steel industrialist [[Henry Phipps Jr.]], opened the [[Phipps Garden Apartments]] at 39th Avenue and 50th Street, on land adjoining Sunnyside Gardens. Designed by Clarence Stein, the original 1931 complex consisted of 22 connected four- and six-story buildings housing 344 families, arranged around a landscaped interior courtyard.<ref name="Marzlock2008">{{Cite news|url=https://www.qchron.com/qboro/i_have_often_walked/the-beautiful-phipps-garden-apts-revisited/article_c7572ff7-b0bc-55a6-93a1-707560edaa2f.html|title=The beautiful Phipps Garden Apts., revisited|last=Marzlock|first=Ron|work=Queens Chronicle|date=November 20, 2008|access-date=April 30, 2026}}</ref><ref name="Plunz1990">{{Cite book|last=Plunz|first=Richard|title=A History of Housing in New York City: Dwelling Type and Social Change in the American Metropolis|publisher=Columbia University Press|year=1990|isbn=978-0-231-06298-5|page=160}}</ref> A second group of thirteen four-story buildings was added on the northern portion of the superblock in 1935.<ref name="ConservancyHistory">{{Cite web|url=https://sunnysidegardens.us/history/|title=History|publisher=Sunnyside Gardens Conservancy|access-date=April 30, 2026|archive-date=September 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250930190843/https://sunnysidegardens.us/history|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="LPC2007">{{Cite report|url=https://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/2258.pdf|title=Sunnyside Gardens Historic District Designation Report|publisher=New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission|date=June 26, 2007|access-date=June 7, 2026|archive-date=January 18, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260118081139/http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/2258.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> 

On August 6, 1931, the jazz cornetist [[Bix Beiderbecke]] died in his apartment at 43-30 46th Street.<ref name="GuardianBix">{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2005/apr/30/popandrock1|title=Solo in Sunnyside|first=Frank|last=Gray|work=The Guardian|date=April 30, 2005|access-date=April 30, 2026|archive-date=April 2, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170402082757/https://www.theguardian.com/music/2005/apr/30/popandrock1|url-status=live}}</ref>

The Depression brought heavy losses to the new homeowners of Sunnyside Gardens; about half lost their homes to foreclosure during the 1930s, and marshals attempting evictions were sometimes met with organized resistance.<ref name="Jackson1266"/> Sunnyside Gardens residents organized rent and mortgage strikes in response to the wave of foreclosures.<ref name="Garb1994"/> The remainder of Sunnyside's prewar apartment stock was completed during the 1930s and 1940s, much of it as middle-income rental housing. In the 1940s and 1950s, the apartments of Sunnyside attracted artists and writers from lower Manhattan in such numbers that the neighborhood became known as the "maternity ward of Greenwich Village".<ref name="Jackson1266"/>
[[File:Site of the Sunnyside Garden Arena Plaque, May 2026.jpg|alt=Short gray plaque that says Site of the Sunnyside Garden Arena|thumb|274x274px|Sunnyside Garden Arena Plaque]]
[[Sunnyside Garden Arena]], at 44-11 Queens Boulevard, operated as a boxing and wrestling venue from the mid-1940s until June 24, 1977. The arena seated about 2,500 spectators and hosted bouts featuring [[Floyd Patterson]], [[Emile Griffith]], [[José Torres (boxer)|José Torres]], and [[Gerry Cooney]], as well as [[Golden Gloves]] tournaments; under owner Michael Rosenberg in the 1970s the venue's programming also extended to karate, dancing, and bingo. [[John F. Kennedy]] delivered a campaign address at the venue on October 27, 1960, less than two weeks before the [[1960 United States presidential election|presidential election]],<ref name="JFKLibrary1960">{{Cite web|url=https://www.jfklibrary.org/archives/other-resources/john-f-kennedy-speeches/queens-ny-19601027|title=Remarks of Senator John F. Kennedy at Sunnyside Gardens, Queens, NY, October 27, 1960|publisher=John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum|access-date=May 1, 2026|archive-date=June 16, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240616080858/https://www.jfklibrary.org/archives/other-resources/john-f-kennedy-speeches/queens-ny-19601027|url-status=live}}</ref> and the [[DuMont Television Network]] broadcast a weekly program, ''Boxing From Sunnyside Gardens'', from the venue from 1949 to 1950.<ref name="MurrayQNS2014">{{Cite news|last=Murray|first=Christian|url=https://qns.com/sunnyside-street-co-named-after-famous-sporting-arena/|title=Sunnyside Street Co-Named After Famous Sporting Arena|work=QNS|date=September 23, 2014|access-date=May 1, 2026}}</ref><ref name="NYT1972">{{Cite news|last=Ingrassia|first=Michele|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1972/04/16/archives/inside-the-ring-or-out-theres-always-action-at-sunnyside.html|title=Inside the Ring or Out, There's Always Action at Sunnyside|work=The New York Times|date=April 16, 1972|page=20|access-date=May 1, 2026}}</ref> The arena was demolished in late 1977; a memorial monument was installed at the former site (now a Wendy's restaurant) in October 2012, and a portion of 45th Street was co-named in its honor in 2014.<ref name="MurrayQNS2014"/><ref name="QNSMonument2012">{{Cite news|url=https://qns.com/2012/10/monument-honors-former-site-of-sunnyside-garden-arena/|title=Monument honors former site of Sunnyside Garden Arena|work=QNS|date=October 17, 2012|access-date=May 1, 2026}}</ref>

===1960s–1990s===
Beginning in the 1960s and accelerating after the [[Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965]], successive waves of immigrants settled in Sunnyside. In July 1977, ''[[The New York Times]]'' reported that Armenian refugees fleeing the [[Lebanese Civil War|civil war in Lebanon]] were resettling in the neighborhood, describing how "the exotic sounds of spoken Armenian have been spreading in the homey sidestreets of Sunnyside, Queens."<ref name="Pace1977">{{Cite news|last=Pace|first=Eric|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1977/07/11/archives/new-yorks-armenian-neighborhoods-feel-a-surge-of-ethnic-pride-as.html|title=New York's Armenian Neighborhoods Feel a Surge of Ethnic Pride as New Immigrant Wave Arrives|work=The New York Times|date=July 11, 1977|page=23|access-date=April 30, 2026}}</ref><ref name="Samuel104">{{Cite book|last=Samuel|first=Lawrence R.|title=Queens: A History of the Most Diverse Place on Earth|publisher=Excelsior Editions|year=2025|page=104}}</ref> In the late 1960s, threats from urban blight and white flight prompted the formation of local civic groups such as Gateway Community Services, which worked to combat crime and improve schools in Sunnyside and adjacent Woodside. Despite these changes, the article observed that Sunnyside "continues to house two and three generations of its original home buyers."<ref name="Garb1994"/> A 1971 ''New York Times'' article characterized Sunnyside as a somewhat marginalized community of 50,000 people that was suffering from a narcotics problem, though it had relatively little violent crime. The article described Sunnyside as a "generally blue collar community, until recently virtually all‐white, mostly Irish‐American, with a sprinkling of Jews. Now there are Colombians and Puerto Ricans and a smattering of blacks."<ref name="Ferretti1971">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1971/06/06/archives/narcotics-are-complicating-sunnysides-problems.html|title=Narcotics Are Complicating Sunnyside's Problems|last=Ferretti|first=Fred|date=June 6, 1971|work=The New York Times|access-date=May 29, 2026}}</ref>

According to ''Ultimate Classic Rock'' and contemporaneous reporting, the rock band [[Kiss (band)|Kiss]] played its first concert on January 30, 1973, at the Coventry (formerly the Popcorn Pub), a small live-music venue at 47-03 Queens Boulevard near 47th Street; the [[Ramones]] also played early shows at the venue.<ref name="UCRKiss">{{Cite web|url=https://ultimateclassicrock.com/kiss-first-concert/|title=50 Years Ago: Kiss Plays Their First Concert|work=Ultimate Classic Rock|date=January 30, 2023|access-date=April 30, 2026|archive-date=April 12, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260412125930/https://ultimateclassicrock.com/kiss-first-concert/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="NYSMusic2025">{{Cite web|url=https://nysmusic.com/2025/06/05/the-story-of-kiss-first-show-and-the-forgotten-queens-venue-behind-it-coventry/|title=The Story of Kiss's First Show and the Forgotten Queens Venue Behind It|website=NYS Music|date=June 5, 2025|access-date=September 11, 2025|archive-date=November 9, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251109054144/https://nysmusic.com/2025/06/05/the-story-of-kiss-first-show-and-the-forgotten-queens-venue-behind-it-coventry/|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Architecture and housing==
Sunnyside's residential building stock dates almost entirely from the [[interwar period]] (roughly 1917–1941). North of [[Queens Boulevard]], the [[Sunnyside Gardens, Queens|Sunnyside Gardens]] development applied the principles of the British [[Garden city movement|garden-city movement]].<ref name="Plunz1990"/>

===Sunnyside Gardens===
{{Main|Sunnyside Gardens, Queens}}
Sunnyside Gardens, built between 1924 and 1928 by the City Housing Corporation, applied the principles of the British garden-city movement at city scale. The development covers 77 acres across about 16 blocks between 43rd and 51st Streets, north of Queens Boulevard.<ref name="HDCSunnyside"/><ref name="Jackson1266"/> Architects [[Clarence Stein]] and [[Henry Wright (planner)|Henry Wright]], working with [[Frederick L. Ackerman]] and the landscape architect [[Marjorie Sewell Cautley]], designed the development "according to ideals of 'health, open space, greenery, and idyllic community living for all'".<ref name="Jackson1266"/> The buildings consist of one-, two-, and three-family attached brick houses with slate roofs, gables, and porches, arranged around open center courts with tree-lined pathways and private and communal flower gardens. Cautley, who designed the gardens, was one of the first female landscape architects in the United States.<ref name="Jackson1266"/> The site comprised 1,202 housing units in a mix of cooperative, rental, and limited-dividend tenures.<ref name="HDCSunnyside"/> Within the development, Sunnyside Gardens Park, a privately owned roughly three-acre common space opened in 1926 and maintained by member-residents, is one of only two private residential parks in New York City, alongside Manhattan's [[Gramercy Park]].<ref name="WilkinsonSunnyside2005">{{Cite web|url=https://forgotten-ny.com/2005/09/sunnyside-queens/|title=Sunnyside, Queens|last=Wilkinson|first=Christina|website=Forgotten New York|date=September 12, 2005|access-date=May 1, 2026|archive-date=October 28, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211028153749/https://forgotten-ny.com/2005/09/sunnyside-queens/|url-status=live}}</ref>

During the [[Great Depression|Depression]] of the 1930s, about half the homeowners of Sunnyside Gardens lost their homes to foreclosure; eviction attempts by city marshals were sometimes met with organized resistance.<ref name="Jackson1266"/> The 40-year covenants that had governed the development's open spaces expired in 1966, after which some residents fenced their rear yards, plastered over brick facades, or built driveways, breaking up several of the original courts.<ref name="Jackson1266"/><ref name="Garb1994"/>

In 1974 the [[New York City Department of City Planning]] designated Sunnyside Gardens a Special Planned Community Preservation District in order to protect the original design.<ref name="Jackson1266"/> The Sunnyside Gardens Conservancy was formed in 1981, and through its advocacy the district was listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]] on September 7, 1984.<ref name="NRHP1984"/><ref name="Jackson1266"/> The [[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]] designated Sunnyside Gardens (including Phipps Garden Apartments) a New York City historic district on June 26, 2007.<ref name="LPC2007"/>

===Phipps Garden Apartments===
{{Main|Phipps Garden Apartments}}
Adjacent to Sunnyside Gardens, on 39th Avenue between 50th and 52nd Streets, the [[Phipps Garden Apartments]] complex was built in two phases by Phipps Houses, the philanthropic real-estate organization established by the family of [[Henry Phipps Jr.]] The first phase, designed by Clarence Stein, opened on September 1, 1931, and consisted of 22 connected four- and six-story buildings housing 344 families arranged around a landscaped interior courtyard.<ref name="Marzlock2008"/> A second northern group of thirteen four-story buildings was completed in 1935.<ref name="ConservancyHistory"/> Half of the buildings are six-story elevator houses; half are four-story walk-ups. Original rents in 1931 ranged from $31 to $80 per month.<ref name="Marzlock2008"/> Phipps Garden Apartments is a contributing property within the Sunnyside Gardens Historic District.<ref name="LPC2007"/>

===Adaptive reuse and other notable buildings===
The former Knickerbocker Laundry Factory at 43-23 37th Avenue, an [[Art Deco]] structure built in 1932, was converted to use as the New York Presbyterian Church in the late 1990s. The conversion was reviewed by [[Herbert Muschamp]] in ''[[The New York Times]]''.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Muschamp|first=Herbert|date=September 5, 1999|title=ART/ARCHITECTURE; A Queens Factory Is Born Again, as a Church|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/09/05/arts/art-architecture-a-queens-factory-is-born-again-as-a-church.html|access-date=April 30, 2026|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=September 15, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250915120706/https://www.nytimes.com/1999/09/05/arts/art-architecture-a-queens-factory-is-born-again-as-a-church.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The [[Celtic_Park_(Queens)|Celtic Park Apartments]], on the site of the former Irish-American Athletic Club athletic field, were built starting in 1931. The nine-acre, 756-unit complex spans 42nd to 44th Streets between 48th and 50th Avenues, straddling the boundary between Sunnyside and adjacent Woodside, and was converted to cooperative ownership in May 1986.<ref name="IrishTimesCelticPark"/><ref name="ParryCelticPark2012">{{Cite news|last=Parry|first=Bill|url=https://qns.com/demand-for-celtic-park-co-ops-picks-up/|title=Demand for Celtic Park Co-ops Picks Up|work=QNS|date=October 2, 2012|access-date=May 1, 2026}}</ref>

{{Main|Sunnyside Arch}}

==Demographics==

Based on data from the [[2020 United States census]], the population of the Sunnyside Neighborhood Tabulation Area (NTA) was 52,278, corresponding to a population density of 47.8 people per acre, slightly denser than New York City's 45.8 people per acre.<ref name="FactFinder2020QN0202">{{cite web |title=Sunnyside (QN0202): Population, Sex, Age, and Density (2020 Decennial Census) |website=New York City Population FactFinder |publisher=New York City Department of City Planning |url=https://popfactfinder.planning.nyc.gov/explorer/ntas/QN0202?acsTopics=demo-sexAndAge%2Cdemo-mutuallyExclusiveRaceHispanicOrigin%2Cdemo-hispanicSubgroup%2Cdemo-asianSubgroup&censusTopics=populationSexAgeDensity%2CmutuallyExclusiveRaceHispanicOrigin%2CdetailedRaceAndEthnicity%2CrelationHeadHousehold%2ChouseholdType%2ChousingOccupancy%2ChousingTenure%2ChouseholdSize&compareTo=0&showCharts=true&showReliability=false&source=decennial-current |access-date=June 2, 2026 |archive-date=June 3, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260603002714/https://popfactfinder.planning.nyc.gov/explorer/ntas/QN0202?acsTopics=demo-sexAndAge%2Cdemo-mutuallyExclusiveRaceHispanicOrigin%2Cdemo-hispanicSubgroup%2Cdemo-asianSubgroup&censusTopics=populationSexAgeDensity%2CmutuallyExclusiveRaceHispanicOrigin%2CdetailedRaceAndEthnicity%2CrelationHeadHousehold%2ChouseholdType%2ChousingOccupancy%2ChousingTenure%2ChouseholdSize&compareTo=0&showCharts=true&showReliability=false&source=decennial-current |url-status=live }}</ref> Depending on the boundaries used, population estimates vary. Citing 2019-2023 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates within its "Sunnyside Context Area", a New York City Department of Small Business Services study reported the neighborhood's population as 49,034.<ref name="SBS-CDNA"/>{{rp|16}} Meanwhile, the New York Comptroller's Office, also citing the 2019-2023 ACS population estimate, reported Sunnyside's population as 47,507.<ref name="OSC2025">{{cite report |title=Long Island City, Sunnyside and Woodside: An Economic Snapshot |publisher=Office of the New York State Comptroller|date=September 2025|url=https://www.osc.ny.gov/files/reports/pdf/report-12-2026.pdf |format=PDF |access-date=2026-05-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260214030116/https://www.osc.ny.gov/files/reports/pdf/report-12-2026.pdf|archive-date=2026-02-14 |url-status=live}}</ref>{{rp|4}}

The racial makeup of the neighborhood was 31.4% (16,395) [[Non-Hispanic or Latino whites|non-Hispanic White]], 3.3% (1,716) [[African American (U.S. Census)|African American]], 25.1% (13,123) [[Asian (U.S. Census)|Asian]], 1.2% (621) [[Race (United States Census)|other races]], 2.8% (1,466) two or more races, and 36.3% (18,957) [[Hispanic (U.S. Census)|Hispanic]] or [[Latino (U.S. Census)|Latino]] of any race.<ref name="FactFinder2020QN0202"/> About 49.6% of residents were born in a US state (37.7% in [[New_York_(state)|New York]]), 3% were born in Puerto Rico, U.S. Island areas, or born abroad to American parent(s), and 47.4% were foreign-born (more than New York City's overall foreign-born share of 36.5% and just below the 47.6% foreign-born share for Queens).<ref name="NTAACS"/>

As of the 2019-2023 American Community Survey, the median [[household income]] in Sunnyside was $80,933, compared to $84,961 in all of Queens and $79,713 in New York City as a whole.<ref name="NTAACS">{{cite web|url=https://popfactfinder.planning.nyc.gov/explorer/ntas/QN0202?acsTopics=all&source=acs-current|title=Population Fact Finder: 1 NTA Queens: Sunnyside [QN0202]|publisher=NYC Planning|access-date=June 6, 2026}}</ref> An estimated 7.9% of residents lived in poverty, compared to 9.4% in Queens and 13.6% in New York City. Among renters, 50% paid more than 30% of their income on rent (vs 52.4% in Queens) and 21.5% paid 50% or more of their income on rent (vs 27.6% in Queens).<ref name="NTAACS" />

The neighborhood has a median age of 38.8 years, versus 40.4 for Queens and 38.0 years for New York City. About 17% of residents are under-18 years old (versus 19.8% for Queens and 20.4% for New York City), and 13.5% are aged 65 years and older (versus 17.2% for Queens and 16.0% for New York City). Twenty-percent of households include children under 18 years old (versus 24.0% in Queens and 23.1% citywide), and 39% of households consisted of a householder alone (versus 26.5% in Queens and 33.4% citywide). The average household size was 2.23 (versus 2.77 in Queens and 2.51 citywide).<ref name="NTAACS" />

==Police and crime==
Woodside, Sunnyside, and Long Island City are patrolled by the 108th Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department|NYPD]], located at 5-47 50th Avenue.<ref name="NYPD 108th Precinct">{{cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/108th-precinct.page|title=NYPD–108th Precinct|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=October 3, 2016|archive-date=May 25, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170525103337/http://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/108th-precinct.page|url-status=live}}</ref> The 108th Precinct ranked 25th safest out of 69 patrol areas for per-capita crime in 2010.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/queens/sunnyside/|title=Sunnyside and Woodside–DNAinfo.com Crime and Safety Report|website=www.dnainfo.com|access-date=October 6, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170415053229/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/queens/sunnyside|archive-date=April 15, 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref> {{As of|2018}}, with a non-fatal assault rate of 19 per 100,000 people, Sunnyside and Woodside's rate of [[violent crime]]s per capita is less than that of the city as a whole. The incarceration rate of 163 per 100,000 people is lower than that of the city as a whole.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|8}}

The 108th Precinct has a lower crime rate than in the 1990s, with crimes across all categories having decreased by 88.2% between 1990 and 2018. The precinct reported 2 murders, 12 rapes, 90 robberies, 108 felony assaults, 109 burglaries, 490 grand larcenies, and 114 grand larcenies auto in 2018.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-108pct.pdf|title=108th Precinct CompStat Report|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=July 22, 2018|archive-date=April 13, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180413202232/http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-108pct.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Health==
{{As of|2018}}, [[preterm birth]]s are more common in Sunnyside and Woodside than in other places citywide, but births to teenage mothers are less common. In Sunnyside and Woodside, there were 90 preterm births per 1,000 live births (compared to 87 per 1,000 citywide), and 14.9 births to teenage mothers per 1,000 live births (compared to 19.3 per 1,000 citywide).<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|11}} Sunnyside and Woodside has a high population of residents who are [[Health insurance coverage in the United States|uninsured]]. In 2018, this population of uninsured residents was estimated to be 16%, which is higher than the citywide rate of 12%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|14}}

The concentration of [[particulates|fine particulate matter]], the deadliest type of [[air pollution|air pollutant]], in Sunnyside and Woodside is {{convert|0.0093|mg/m3|oz/ft3}}, higher than the city average.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|9}} Fourteen percent of Sunnyside and Woodside residents are [[Smoking|smokers]], which is equal to the city average of 14% of residents being smokers.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} In Sunnyside and Woodside, 20% of residents are [[Obesity|obese]], 9% are [[Diabetes mellitus|diabetic]], and 23% have [[hypertension|high blood pressure]]—compared to the citywide averages of 20%, 14%, and 24% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|16}} In addition, 19% of children are obese, compared to the citywide average of 20%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|12}}

Ninety-two percent of residents eat some fruits and vegetables every day, which is higher than the city's average of 87%. In 2018, 79% of residents described their health as "good", "very good", or "excellent", slightly higher than the city's average of 78%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} For every supermarket in Sunnyside and Woodside, there are 17 [[convenience store|bodegas]].<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|10}}

The nearest large hospitals in the area are the [[Elmhurst Hospital Center]] in [[Elmhurst, Queens|Elmhurst]] and the [[Mount Sinai Hospital (Manhattan)|Mount Sinai Hospital of Queens]] in [[Astoria, Queens|Astoria]].<ref>{{cite web | last=Finkel | first=Beth | title=Guide To Queens Hospitals | website=Queens Tribune | date=February 27, 2014 | url=http://queenstribune.com/guide-to-queens-hospitals/ | access-date=March 7, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170204185507/http://queenstribune.com/guide-to-queens-hospitals/ | archive-date=February 4, 2017 | url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Education ==
[[File:PS150 43rd Av jeh.JPG|thumb|PS 150]]
Sunnyside and Woodside generally has a slightly higher ratio of college-educated residents than the rest of the city {{as of|2018|lc=y}}. While 45% of residents age 25 and older have a college education or higher, 19% have less than a high school education and 35% are high school graduates or have some college education. By contrast, 39% of Queens residents and 43% of city residents have a college education or higher.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} The percentage of Sunnyside and Woodside students excelling in math rose from 40% in 2000 to 65% in 2011, and reading achievement rose from 45% to 49% during the same time period.<ref name=":17">{{cite web|url=http://furmancenter.org/files/sotc/QN_02_11.pdf|title=Woodside and Sunnyside–QN 02|date=2011|publisher=[[Furman Center for Real Estate and Urban Policy]]|access-date=October 5, 2016|archive-date=September 18, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130918205201/http://furmancenter.org/files/sotc/QN_02_11.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

Sunnyside and Woodside's rate of elementary school student absenteeism is less than the rest of New York City. In Sunnyside and Woodside, 11% of elementary school students missed twenty or more days per [[school year]], lower than the citywide average of 20%.<ref name=":21" />{{Rp|24 (PDF p. 55)}}<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} Additionally, 86% of high school students in Sunnyside and Woodside graduate on time, more than the citywide average of 75%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}}

===St. Pats for All Parade===
{{Main|St. Pat's for All}}
Portions of the neighborhood are along the route of the annual [[St. Pat's for All]] parade, an inclusive [[Saint Patrick's Day]] celebration founded in 2000 by Brendan Fay and Ellen Duncan in response to the exclusion of [[LGBT]] Irish groups from the [[New York City St. Patrick's Day Parade|Manhattan St. Patrick's Day Parade]] by the [[Ancient Order of Hibernians]]. The inaugural parade on March 5, 2000, drew First Lady [[Hillary Clinton]] and Father [[Mychal Judge]] among its marchers, and proceeds along Skillman Avenue between 43rd Street in Sunnyside and 58th Street in adjacent [[Woodside, Queens|Woodside]]. Its slogan, "Cherishing All the Children of the Nation Equally," derives from the [[Proclamation of the Irish Republic]] of the 1916 [[Easter Rising]].<ref name="NYCLGBTStPats">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nyclgbtsites.org/site/starting-point-of-first-st-pats-for-all-parade/|title=St. Pat's for All Parade|last=Davis|first=Amanda|publisher=NYC LGBTQ Historic Sites Project|date=January 2019|access-date=May 1, 2026|archive-date=March 17, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260317174823/https://www.nyclgbtsites.org/site/starting-point-of-first-st-pats-for-all-parade/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://qns.com/2026/02/st-pats-for-all-parade-sunnyside-march/|title=St. Pat's for All Parade celebrating inclusivity and Irish heritage to return March 1 in Sunnyside|last=O'Brien|first=Shane|work=QNS|date=February 19, 2026|access-date=April 30, 2026|archive-date=May 18, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260518215715/https://qns.com/2026/02/st-pats-for-all-parade-sunnyside-march/|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Transportation==

===Subway and bus===
[[File:NYC Subway 7 express train.jpg|thumb|7 trains at [[40th Street–Lowery Street (IRT Flushing Line)|40th Street–Lowery Street]] station]]
Sunnyside is served by the {{NYCS trains|Flushing local}} on the [[New York City Subway]]'s [[IRT Flushing Line]] at three local-only stations: [[33rd Street–Rawson Street (IRT Flushing Line)|33rd Street–Rawson Street]], [[40th Street–Lowery Street (IRT Flushing Line)|40th Street–Lowery Street]], and [[46th Street–Bliss Street (IRT Flushing Line)|46th Street–Bliss Street]]. Express service on the line runs in the peak direction during rush hours between [[Queensboro Plaza (IRT Flushing Line)|Queensboro Plaza]] and [[Mets–Willets Point (IRT Flushing Line)|Mets–Willets Point]]; express trains pass through the three Sunnyside stations without stopping. The nearest express stop is [[61st Street–Woodside (IRT Flushing Line)|61st Street–Woodside]], one stop east of the neighborhood.<ref name="MTA7">{{Cite web|url=https://www.mta.info/maps/subway-line-maps/7-line|title=7 Line Map|publisher=Metropolitan Transportation Authority|access-date=April 30, 2026|archive-date=May 15, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260515150834/https://www.mta.info/maps/subway-line-maps/7-line|url-status=live}}</ref>

The {{NYC bus link|Q32|Q39|Q60|Q67|Q104|prose=y|B24}} buses operate within Sunnyside, with the Q32 and Q60 running along Queens Boulevard.

===Roads===
The neighborhood is connected to [[Manhattan]] via the [[Long Island Expressway]] and the [[Queens–Midtown Tunnel]] and to [[Brooklyn]] via the [[Brooklyn–Queens Expressway]]. [[Queens Boulevard]], a wide multi-lane arterial, runs through the middle of the neighborhood.

===Bicycle infrastructure===
In 2018 the [[New York City Department of Transportation]] installed parking-protected bicycle lanes on Skillman and 43rd Avenues, replacing curbside parking with separated bike lanes between approximately 43rd Street and 50th Street. The project followed the November 2017 death of cyclist Gelacio Reyes, who was struck by a driver on 43rd Avenue. After several years of public hearings in which [[Queens Community Board 2]] voted against the proposal and Council Member [[Jimmy Van Bramer]] initially withheld support, Mayor [[Bill de Blasio]] directed the Department of Transportation to proceed and construction began in August 2018.<ref name="Kuntzman2018"/>

[[Citi Bike]] docking stations were installed across Sunnyside and adjacent Woodside in spring 2022 as part of the system's expansion into western Queens, with about 71 stations planned for the two neighborhoods.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://sunnysidepost.com/dot-to-rollout-citi-bike-in-sunnyside-woodside-by-may-about-70-stations-to-be-installed|title=DOT to Rollout Citi Bike in Sunnyside/Woodside by May, About 70 Stations to be Installed|work=Sunnyside Post|date=February 2, 2022|access-date=April 30, 2026|archive-date=August 5, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250805114630/https://sunnysidepost.com/dot-to-rollout-citi-bike-in-sunnyside-woodside-by-may-about-70-stations-to-be-installed|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Rail and ferry===
[[Sunnyside Yard]], built by the [[Pennsylvania Railroad]] and now owned by [[Amtrak]], occupies the northern edge of the neighborhood and serves as a staging facility for [[Amtrak]] and [[NJ Transit Rail Operations|NJ Transit]] trains using [[Pennsylvania Station (New York City)|Pennsylvania Station]].<ref name="Couper1912"/>

A passenger station at Sunnyside has been a long-standing proposal. The [[East Side Access]] project's 2001 environmental impact statement contemplated a [[Long Island Rail Road]] station at Queens Boulevard and Skillman Avenue, and the [[Metropolitan Transportation Authority]]'s 2025–2044 20-year needs assessment included a cost evaluation for a station at the same location to be served by both the Long Island Rail Road and [[Metro-North Railroad]] following completion of the [[Penn Station Access]] project.<ref name="MTA20Year">{{Cite report|url=https://future.mta.info/documents/20-YearNeedsAssessment_ReportandAppendix.pdf|title=20-Year Needs Assessment 2025–2044, Report and Appendix|publisher=Metropolitan Transportation Authority|date=January 2025|page=254|access-date=April 30, 2026|archive-date=May 31, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260531195109/https://future.mta.info/documents/20-YearNeedsAssessment_ReportandAppendix.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> A Sunnyside station is not part of the funded scope of Penn Station Access, which provides four new Metro-North stations in the [[East Bronx]]; that project is currently expected to be substantially complete in 2030.<ref name="Colon2025">{{Cite news|url=https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2025/10/28/amtraks-dithering-delays-completion-of-penn-access-to-2030-mta-says|title=Amtrak's Dithering Delays Completion of Penn Access to 2030, MTA Says|last=Colon|first=Dave|work=Streetsblog NYC|date=October 28, 2025|access-date=April 30, 2026}}</ref>

The nearest [[NYC Ferry]] landing is at [[Hunters Point South]] in [[Long Island City]], approximately one mile west of southern Sunnyside.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ferry.nyc/routes-and-schedules/|title=Routes and Schedules|publisher=NYC Ferry|date=2026|access-date=April 30, 2026|archive-date=January 1, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240101210325/https://www.ferry.nyc/routes-and-schedules/|url-status=live}}</ref>
